headline: Monthly GDP Contracts 0.6% as Manufacturing Falls 4.6% YoY, BoC Holds at 2.25%
executive_summary:
Statistics Canada's monthly real GDP by industry print recorded a -0.6%180 month-over-month contraction, with manufacturing GDP down 1.4% month-over-month and -4.6% year-over-year and management of companies and enterprises (NAICS 55) down 4.1% month-over-month and -21.9% year-over-year, the deepest annual contraction among 20 tracked industries.180 Construction GDP rose 1.1% month-over-month and 2.8% year-over-year, partially offsetting the broader monthly decline. The project database tracks 52 manufacturing projects ($67.4B) and 1,687 infrastructure projects ($179.0B) in the affected NAICS sectors.

The Bank of Canada overnight rate held at 2.25%73 following the March 5, 2026 decision, the seventh consecutive hold at this level. The prime rate sits at 6.09%177 and the 2-year Government of Canada yield at 2.95%, approximately 70 basis points above the policy rate.177 The next BoC decision is scheduled for April 16, 2026. Headline CPI registered +1.8%178 year-over-year in March, within the central bank's 1-3% target band, with a 6.5 percentage-point provincial dispersion ranging from PE +5.4% to ON -1.1% and SK -0.7%.178

The Labour Force Survey recorded national unemployment at 6.7%179 in March 2026, with a 4.5 percentage-point provincial spread between Saskatchewan at 5.0% (lowest) and Newfoundland and Labrador at 9.5% (highest).179 Construction employment stood at 1,998,800, manufacturing employment at 249,600, and mining and oil and gas extraction employment at 350,300.183 The participation rate carried at 64.9% from the February observation, 71 days old at the time of refresh.179

Brent crude settled at US$96.52/bbl184 on April 9, 2026, down 11.47% week-over-week and up 47.40% year-over-year. The WTI Yahoo scrape was flagged as unreliable this week and is not cited. Statistics Canada's Non-residential Capital and Repair Expenditures release places 2026 capital expenditure intentions at $401.2B181, of which $274.0B is construction and $127.2B machinery and equipment.181 The pipeline tracks 7,344 active projects worth $1,366.6B across 13 provinces and territories. The Bank of Canada April 16 rate decision and the federal budget release scheduled on or about April 15 follow next week, alongside the March CPI release on April 17.

national.analysis:
Canada's monthly real GDP by industry contracted -0.6%180 in the latest Statistics Canada print, reversing the prior month's +0.1% reading. Manufacturing GDP (NAICS 31-33) fell 1.4% month-over-month and 4.6% year-over-year, the steepest goods-producing decline in the release. Management of companies and enterprises (NAICS 55) recorded the deepest annual contraction in the table at -21.9% year-over-year and -4.1% month-over-month.180 Construction (NAICS 23) rose 1.1% month-over-month and 2.8% year-over-year, while mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction (NAICS 21) gained 1.2% month-over-month against a -0.1% annual base.180 Wholesale trade (NAICS 41) declined 1.2% month-over-month and 1.7% year-over-year; transportation and warehousing (NAICS 48-49) fell 0.7% month-over-month against a +1.6% annual base.180

The Labour Force Survey recorded unemployment at 6.7%179 in March 2026, unchanged from the prior print. Employment fell 84,000 in February after gaining 76,000 in January, with full-time employment down 108,000 and part-time employment up 24,000.179 Private sector employment fell 73,000 and public sector employment fell 11,000.179 Industry-level employment from Table 14-10-0022 placed construction employment at 1,998,800, manufacturing at 249,600, and mining and oil and gas extraction at 350,300.183 Wage growth ran at +3.9% year-over-year per Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours data.193 The participation rate carried at 64.9%, observed February 1, 2026 and 71 days old at the time of this refresh.179

Headline CPI rose 1.8%178 year-over-year in March 2026, down 0.5 percentage points from the prior print. Provincial CPI dispersion spans 6.5 percentage points: PE +5.4%, AB +3.4%, MB +3.1%, NL +1.8%, NS +1.5%, NB +1.2%, BC +1.0%, QC +0.6%, SK -0.7%, and ON -1.1%.178 Core CPI median ran at 2.3%, shelter CPI at +1.5%, food CPI at 5.3%, and energy CPI at -14.2%.178 Statistics Canada's January merchandise trade report placed the trade deficit at $3.6B, widened from $1.3B, with exports down 4.7% to $62.5B and imports down 1.1% to $66.1B; motor vehicle exports fell 21.2%. January retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7B, with motor vehicle dealers up 2.0% and core retail (ex gasoline and motor vehicles) up 0.9%; the advance February estimate was +0.9%.

CMHC housing starts ran at 250,900 SAAR110, up 4.5% from the prior print of 240,148. Building permits totalled $13.3B194 in January, up 4.8%, of which residential permits were $25.9B (annualized basis) and non-residential $10.3B.194 Statistics Canada's Non-residential Capital and Repair Expenditures release places 2026 capital expenditure intentions at $401.2B181, of which $274.0B is construction and $127.2B machinery and equipment.181 The pipeline tracks 211 residential projects ($44.4B), 1,687 infrastructure projects ($179.0B), and a total of 7,344 active projects worth $1,366.6B.

provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate held at 7.6% in the February Labour Force Survey, +0.3 percentage points from the prior month and the highest provincial print in Central Canada73. The participation rate rose +0.2 percentage points to 64.6% while the employment rate held flat at 59.7%, below the national 60.6% figure73. The provincial CPI series printed at -1.1% year-over-year, the lowest provincial CPI reading in the country177. Housing starts came in at 67,274 units (CMHC seasonally adjusted annualized), up from 65,757 the prior month178.

Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy tabled the Ontario Budget 2026 on March 26, raising the ten-year capital plan to over $210 billion, with $37 billion for 2026-27 and approximately $64 billion over ten years for health infrastructure including ~50 hospital projects and ~3,000 new beds179. The budget added $300 million to the Community Sport and Recreation Infrastructure Fund and confirmed $31 billion over ten years for highway investment, with work underway on Highway 413, the Bradford Bypass, the Highway 7 expansion between Kitchener and Guelph, the Garden City Skyway twinning, and Highway 401 upgrades180. The project database tracks 647 Ontario projects valued at $254.4B, of which 234 are Under Construction, 153 Proposed, 94 Approved, and 30 Under Review; infrastructure (198), healthcare (134), and transit and rail (128) are the largest sector categories110.

The Adaptive Phased Management Deep Geological Repository ($26.0B, Proposed, Nuclear Waste Management Organization) remains in the federal Impact Assessment Registry, alongside the Ontario Line ($27.4B, Under Construction) and GO Expansion ($26.1B, Under Construction) as the province's largest active capital files181. Ontario building permits stood at $2,690.8M in the latest StatCan print183. The Bank of Canada delivers its next interest rate decision on April 16, which is tracked alongside Ontario's rate-sensitive residential and infrastructure pipeline182.

The Quebec Treasury Board tabled the Plan québécois des infrastructures 2026-2036 on March 18, totalling $167 billion over ten years with $12.6 billion in new funding for health and social services, education, higher education, and public transit179. Bill 5, advanced through the National Assembly in March, creates a fast-track regulatory pathway for 'priority national-scale projects' assessed on prosperity, autonomy, Indigenous consultation, energy-transition targets, and short-term implementability criteria180. The project database tracks 490 Quebec projects valued at $89.3B, of which 281 are Approved, 86 Under Review, 83 Proposed, and 39 Under Construction110. Education (118), infrastructure (103), and healthcare (49) are the largest sector categories.

Anchor capital files include the Parc éolien zone Chamouchouane ($9.0B, Proposed, Hydro-Québec/MRC Domaine du Roy), the Quebec Transport Infrastructure Investment Plan ($8.0B, Proposed), the revised Montreal Metro Blue Line Extension ($4.89B, Under Construction, STM), the TES Canada green hydrogen facility at Shawinigan ($4.0B, Under Review), and the Québec City Tramway TramCité project ($3.76B, Under Construction)181.

provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.analysis:
Alberta's unemployment rate printed at 6.3% in the February Labour Force Survey, -0.1 percentage points from January, while the participation rate fell -0.3 percentage points to 68.7% and the employment rate fell -0.1 percentage points to 64.4%73. Alberta's participation rate remains the highest in the country, consistent with sustained resource-sector labour demand. The provincial CPI series printed at +3.4% year-over-year, the highest provincial CPI reading in Canada177. Housing starts came in at 48,438 units in the latest CMHC release, down from 48,896 the prior month178. Provincial GDP printed at +2.7%.

The Federal-Alberta-Pathways Alliance tri-lateral Memorandum of Understanding targeted April 1 for a multi-phased framework on the proposed $16.5 billion carbon capture and storage trunkline in northern Alberta, covering carbon-price alignment and CCS financing179. The Pathways Alliance rebranded to the 'Oil Sands Alliance' in February180. The Pathways Alliance CO2 Transportation Network and Storage Hub Project (IAAC Registry entry 89090) is currently in planning phase181. The project database tracks 724 Alberta projects valued at $349.6B — the second-largest provincial pipeline by total value — with 384 Proposed, 172 Under Construction, 83 Complete, 63 Under Review, and 20 Approved; government (146), power and energy (124), and infrastructure (113) are the largest sector categories110.

Anchor capital files include the Alberta Budget 2026 Capital Plan ($28.3B, Proposed)182, the Telus Infrastructure Upgrades province-wide 2023-2027 ($19.0B, Under Construction), the Pathways Alliance CCS Hub Phase 1 ($16.5B, Proposed), and AOSP Jackpine ($12.0B, Approved, Canadian Natural Resources Limited)110181. The Bank of Canada delivers its next rate decision on April 16, which is tracked alongside the energy sector's capex sensitivity183.

Ford's Bécancour cathode plant is expected to begin production in 2026 with up to 45,000 tonnes CAM/yr, and the GM/POSCO Future M Ultium CAM plant is approximately two-thirds complete; the Northvolt and Umicore Kingston projects are on hold, and the Quebec government has committed $270M to the Northvolt project whose status is uncertain.3,4 The SLX steel ETF proxy closed at $90.13, up 1.2% week-over-week and 48.9% year-over-year, a direct input cost for primary metals and transportation equipment subsectors.180 The project database tracks 52 manufacturing-tagged projects totalling $67.39B declared, a thin bucket relative to sector weight; coverage of the battery and EV chemicals pipeline is partial.110 If Ford's Bécancour cathode plant commissions on schedule in 2026 and the GM/POSCO Ultium CAM plant reaches production in early 2026, the battery-chemicals subsector of the 52 tracked manufacturing projects would carry updated status attribution.

industry_executive_summary:
Canadian industry GDP for January 2026 recorded mixed sector-level movement across the 20 NAICS industries — five goods-producing industries and fifteen services industries reported by Statistics Canada174. Among goods producers, Construction (NAICS 23) posted +1.1% month-over-month and +2.8% year-over-year, and Mining, Quarrying & Oil and Gas Extraction (21) rose +1.2% M/M with -0.1% Y/Y. Utilities (22) printed +0.6% M/M and -1.7% Y/Y. Manufacturing (31-33) contracted -1.4% M/M and -4.6% Y/Y, and Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing & Hunting (11) recorded -1.4% M/M with +5.4% Y/Y174.

Services output was led by Information & Cultural Industries and Retail Trade — Information & Cultural Industries (51) posted +0.9% M/M and +3.2% Y/Y, Retail Trade (44-45) +0.8% M/M and +2.7% Y/Y, Accommodation & Food Services (72) +0.7% M/M and +2.3% Y/Y, Finance & Insurance (52) +0.5% M/M and +3.2% Y/Y, and Educational Services (61) +0.5% M/M with -1.9% Y/Y. Health Care & Social Assistance (62) was flat M/M at +0.0% and +2.1% Y/Y, and Other Services (81) added +0.2% M/M and +0.3% Y/Y. Declines were recorded in Wholesale Trade (41) at -1.2% M/M and -1.7% Y/Y, Transportation & Warehousing (48-49) at -0.7% M/M and +1.6% Y/Y, Real Estate & Rental/Leasing (53) at -0.2% M/M and +1.2% Y/Y, Arts, Entertainment & Recreation (71) at -0.1% M/M and +2.2% Y/Y, Professional, Scientific & Technical Services (54) at -0.1% M/M and -0.4% Y/Y, Administrative & Waste Management (56) at -0.1% M/M and -0.2% Y/Y, Public Administration (91) at -0.1% M/M and +0.7% Y/Y, and Management of Companies & Enterprises (55) at -4.1% M/M and -21.9% Y/Y174.

Consumer-facing data points centred on the 1.8%178 headline CPI and the 6.5 percentage-point provincial inflation spread between PE at +5.4% and ON at -1.1%.178 Shelter CPI ran at +1.5%, food CPI at +5.3%, and core CPI median at 2.3%, while energy CPI fell 14.2% year-over-year.178 Average home price stood at $663,828 per CREA data, with January retail sales of $70.7B (+1.1% month-over-month) and an advance February estimate of +0.9% month-over-month. Motor vehicle dealers led January retail with a +2.0% gain, and core retail (ex gasoline and motor vehicles) rose 0.9%.

The Conference Board of Canada consumer confidence index registered 47.50 in February, down 1.80 points from 49.30 in January. The Bloomberg-Nanos index recorded a three-week slide into late March. The Labour Force Survey placed national unemployment at 6.7%179, with the provincial spread running from SK 5.0% to NL 9.5%.179 February employment fell 84,000, with full-time employment down 108,000, part-time employment up 24,000, private sector employment down 73,000, and public sector employment down 11,000.179 Wage growth ran at +3.9% year-over-year per the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, 2.1 percentage points above headline CPI.193 Word-cloud topics captured this week included PE inflation above 5%, ON CPI -1.1%, BoC overnight rate at 2.25%, prime rate 6.09%, housing affordability, NL unemployment 9.5%, manufacturing GDP -4.6% YoY, capex intentions of $401.2B, and uranium proxies up 130% year-over-year.

sections.headline: Strait of Hormuz Crisis Drives WTI Above $100 as Canada Posts 0.1% GDP Growth and 84,000 Job Losses
sections.edition: EDITION: Mar 31 â€“ Apr 6 // STATUS: AI-SYNTHESIZED
sections.executive_summary:
The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since approximately March 2 â€” disrupting an estimated 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows, roughly 20% of global seaborne trade â€” drove WTI crude to US$102.88/bbl on March 30, the first settlement above $100 since July 2022.104 Brent crude surged approximately 55% in March to US$112.78/bbl, a record monthly gain for the contract since inception in 1988.104 The Dallas Federal Reserve estimated that a one-quarter closure could raise WTI to a $98/bbl average and reduce global GDP growth by an annualized 2.9 percentage points in Q2 2026.108 The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects and 785 power and energy projects across Canada, with Alberta accounting for 727 tracked projects that include upstream oil and gas operations.

Statistics Canada reported that employment declined by 84,000 (-0.4%) in February, reversing Q4 2025 gains.144 Full-time employment fell 108,000, private-sector employment dropped 73,000, and the unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January.144 Services-producing industries lost 56,000 positions and goods-producing industries lost 28,000, with wholesale and retail trade recording the largest subsector decline at 18,000 jobs.144 The database tracks 1,034 projects currently under construction that depend on labour market conditions.

Real GDP rose 0.1% in January 2026, marking a second consecutive monthly increase, according to Statistics Canada.149 Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction expanded 1.2%, while manufacturing contracted 1.4%.149 The advance estimate indicates 0.2% growth in February.149 Headline CPI fell to 1.8% year-over-year in February â€” the lowest since early 2021 â€” with core measures converging near 2.3-2.4%.145 The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18, citing weaker near-term growth from US tariffs and stating it would "proceed carefully" given heightened uncertainty.67

The merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December, as motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion â€” the lowest since September 2021.143 Energy exports partially offset the decline, rising 4.1%.143 The April 2 release of February trade data will be the first full month reflecting the Strait of Hormuz closure. On April 3, Statistics Canada releases the March Labour Force Survey, and on April 15, the Bank of Canada delivers its next rate decision alongside the full Monetary Policy Report and March CPI data.69150

national.analysis:
Statistics Canada reported real GDP grew 0.1% in January 2026, a second consecutive monthly increase following a flat December.149 Goods-producing industries expanded 0.2%, led by mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, which grew 1.2% in the month.149 Services-producing industries were essentially unchanged. Manufacturing contracted 1.4%, the steepest monthly decline in the current data cycle, reflecting weakness in both durable and non-durable goods production.149 Retail trade GDP rose 0.8%.149 The advance estimate for February indicates 0.2% growth.78 Q4 2025 GDP contracted 0.2% on an annualized basis, while full-year 2025 GDP growth was approximately 1.7%; the IMF projects 1.6% for 2026.13970

The labour market recorded a contraction of 84,000 positions in February, the largest monthly decline since the pandemic recovery period.144 Full-time employment fell 108,000 while part-time employment rose 24,000. Private-sector employment dropped 73,000. The unemployment rate increased to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January, and the participation rate declined 0.1 percentage points to 64.9%.144 Services-producing industries shed 56,000 positions, with wholesale and retail trade losing 18,000 and other services declining 14,000. Goods-producing industries lost 28,000 positions.14434 Payroll employment from the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH) rose 45,600 (+0.2%) in January, providing a contrasting signal from the establishment survey.140

Headline CPI decelerated to 1.8% year-over-year in February 2026, down from 2.3% in January â€” the lowest reading since early 2021.145 All three Bank of Canada core measures converged: CPI-median at 2.3%, CPI-trim at 2.3%, and CPI-common at 2.4%.145 Food inflation slowed to 5.3% from 7.3% in January.9033 The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18 â€” the seventh consecutive meeting at this level following seven cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.67 Bond markets priced approximately 86% probability of no change at the April 15 meeting.68

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December.143 Total exports fell 4.7% to $62.5 billion; imports declined 1.1% to $66.1 billion. Motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion, the lowest since September 2021, while energy product exports rose 4.1%.14335 Housing starts ran at 250,900 SAAR in February, up 4.5% from 240,148 in January, while the six-month trend declined 0.4% to 256,005 units.89 The average home price stood at $663,828 in February (+1.7% month-over-month).62 Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, with motor vehicle dealers leading at +2.0% and general merchandise retailers posting a fourth consecutive monthly increase at +3.0%.14676 Consumer confidence declined to 47.50 in February from 49.30 in January, while the Bloomberg/Nanos index showed a three-week slide into late March.5748

US equity markets were dominated by Strait of Hormuz-related volatility in March. The S&P 500 stood at approximately 6,496 on March 31, down roughly 9.4% from its January 2026 peak.61 Reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks on March 31 triggered a broad rally: the S&P 500 gained 2.40%, the Nasdaq 3.24%, and the Dow approximately 2.0% on the session.103 Canada's merchandise trade with the US recorded a 21.2% decline in motor vehicle and parts exports to $5.4 billion in January â€” the lowest since September 2021 â€” directly linked to tariff-related disruptions.143

global.analysis:
China's official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.4 in March 2026, crossing above the 50.0 expansion threshold after two months of contraction (49.3 in January, 49.0 in February).105 The non-manufacturing PMI increased to 50.1 from 49.5, with new export orders showing strength.105 The People's Bank of China held the 5-year Loan Prime Rate at 2.90%. China recorded GDP growth of 5.0% for 2025, meeting the official annual target for a second consecutive year. CPI registered +0.2% year-over-year in February, reflecting subdued domestic demand.

China is Canada's second-largest merchandise trading partner, receiving approximately 5% of Canadian merchandise exports annually â€” crude oil, canola, potash, wood products, and seafood are the primary categories. The return to manufacturing expansion after two months of contraction could affect demand for these Canadian commodity exports through Q2 2026. Higher shipping costs from the Strait of Hormuz closure are affecting input prices for Chinese manufacturers and raising transport costs for Canadian LNG and commodity shipments routed to Asia.37 China controls an estimated 60% of global rare earth mine production and approximately 85% of downstream processing, a factor for Canadian critical minerals projects tracked in the database â€” the database contains 364 mining projects across Canada.

provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 7.6% in February 2026144, the highest level in the province since early 2021, as the labour market absorbed the combined effects of U.S. tariff uncertainty on trade-exposed manufacturing and a slowdown in residential construction activity. Toronto CMA housing starts declined 28% year-over-year in February100, reflecting elevated borrowing costs and reduced buyer qualification volumes. The project database tracks 652 Ontario projects, of which 220 are in rate-sensitive sectors11 â€” residential, commercial, and mixed-use developments whose timelines are directly linked to financing conditions and mortgage rate movements.

The Ontario 2026 Budget, released March 26, introduced a $210 billion 10-year capital plan â€” the largest in provincial history â€” with $37 billion allocated for fiscal year 2026-27.28 Of that total, $63 billion is directed to transit expansion (Ontario Line, Yonge North Subway Extension, Scarborough Subway Extension, Hamilton LRT), $64 billion to health infrastructure covering 50+ hospital projects and approximately 3,000 new beds, and $31 billion to highways including Highway 413 (now under construction) and the Bradford Bypass.10647 The budget projects a $13.8 billion deficit for 2026-27, with total spending of $244.2 billion against revenues of $231.9 billion.28

A temporary HST rebate on new homes is estimated to generate 8,000 housing starts and provide $2.2 billion in joint tax relief.28 The Eglinton Crosstown LRT opened in February 2026, delivering 19 km of rapid transit including 10 km underground.125 The small business corporate income tax rate was reduced from 3.2% to 2.2%, with estimated relief of $1.1 billion to over 375,000 small businesses over three years.28 A $4 billion Protect Ontario Account Investment Fund targets AI, defence, advanced manufacturing, and life sciences.130 The database tracks 150 projects in employment-sensitive sectors (healthcare, education, manufacturing, government) and 205 infrastructure projects in Ontario.11

New Brunswick Budget 2026-27 projects a $1.33 billion deficit, with health spending rising $710 million year-over-year.154 Capital spending is increasing from $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion, a $300 million expansion.154 Net debt is projected to rise from $13.9 billion to $19.7 billion by FY2029.154 The database tracks 204 New Brunswick projects, with 45 infrastructure projects and 16 energy-sector projects.26

The nuclear energy sector is a key development area for New Brunswick. NB Power and ARC Clean Technology are advancing the Point Lepreau Small Modular Reactor (ARC-100) proposal, and an NB Power review recommended building a second large nuclear plant adjacent to Point Lepreau.126 Medical isotope production is also being explored at the Point Lepreau site.126 ProEnergy Canada has proposed a $3.5 billion power generation facility in the Tantramar region near Moncton.63 The Saint John Pulp Mill Upgrades ($1.1 billion) are under review at Natural Resources Canada.49

provinces.analysis:
Newfoundland and Labrador's unemployment rate held steady at 9.2% in February 2026144, the highest among all provinces, while employment increased by 2,100 positions (+0.8%) â€” one of only two provinces to record employment gains during the month.144 The simultaneous increase in employment and unchanged unemployment rate indicates that labour force entrants matched the pace of job creation. The CPI index edged up to 166.4 from 166.2.144

The Bay du Nord offshore oil project â€” estimated at $14 billion in total investment â€” reached life-of-field agreements on benefits, royalties, and equity with Equinor and BP in March 2026.120 The agreement includes government revenue of up to $6.4 billion from Phase 1, with production capacity of 160,000-175,000 bbl/d and first oil expected in 2031.120 Over the 25-year project life, Bay du Nord is projected to generate 31 million person-hours of work.120 Offshore oil contributes approximately 20% of provincial GDP and 55% of total exports, sustaining approximately 20,000 jobs.119

The project database tracks 1,549 Newfoundland and Labrador projects and 144 energy-sector projects.27 The Grassy Point LNG project ($10 billion) remains in proposed status.49 The White Rose expansion ($3.8 billion West component and $2.3 billion North/South components) is under construction offshore Newfoundland.49 The Kamistiatusset (Kami) iron ore project ($3.9 billion) in Labrador West is under review.49 Net debt is projected at $19.4 billion (44.7% of GDP).119

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.analysis:
Prince Edward Island's unemployment rate fell 0.4 percentage points to 7.2% in February 2026144, as employment reached an all-time high of 96,200 â€” the highest level on record for the province.132 Population increased 1.6% to 182,657 (through July 2025), international exports rose 12.8%, and tourism overnight stays increased 4.5%, all contributing to employment demand.132

PEI's capital budget for 2026-27 allocates $486.5 million for the fiscal year and $1.6 billion over five years.95 The five-year plan includes $538 million for healthcare infrastructure, $65.4 million for three new elementary schools, and $100 million for more than 300 new affordable housing units plus $28 million for upgrades and repairs to existing public housing stock.95 The Mental Health Campus project ($131 million) is under construction with completion targeted for 2027-28.107

The current 2025-26 forecast deficit has widened to $367.4 million, a $183.4 million increase from the original budget.132 The spring legislature opened March 25 with budget cuts anticipated. No 2026-27 operating budget has been tabled as of March 31.132 The project database tracks 96 PEI projects, with 20 employment-sensitive projects and 43 rate-sensitive projects.1

provinces.analysis:
Yukon's unemployment rate stood at 3.6% in January 2026, the lowest among all provinces and territories141, while the labour force participation rate of 74.4% was the highest in Canada.141 These figures indicate the territory's labour market is operating near full capacity. GDP is projected to decline 2.3% in 2025 before a recovery supported by mineral prices.157

Yukon Budget 2026-27 totals $2.46 billion with a projected $81.8 million deficit and a capital budget of $385 million.157 The federal government announced a $40 billion Northern Defence and Infrastructure Investment package that includes Yukon forward operating locations, military upgrades, roads, and hydro-power expansion.155 The Whitehorse Power Centres Project proposes two new thermal power centres offering up to 150 megawatts through LNG and diesel, with the south centre targeted for winter 2027 and the north centre for winter 2028.79

The Casino Mine ($3.6 billion), located 150 km northwest of Carmacks, remains in proposed status.49 The Kudz Ze Kayah metals mining project ($489 million) is under IAAC review.49 The Yukon government announced initiatives to improve energy grid reliability, with an estimated $1 billion in grid investment proposed.156 The project database tracks 125 Yukon projects, with 15 employment-sensitive projects and 60 rate-sensitive projects.2

provinces.name: Northwest Territories
provinces.analysis:
The Northwest Territories' unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 5.3% in February 2026144, as the territory contends with a structural transition in its resource economy. All three producing diamond mines â€” Diavik (closing 2026), Ekati (2029), and Gahcho Kue (2030) â€” are scheduled to cease operations by 2030, removing a primary employer and revenue source.137 Employment decreased 3.4% between 2023 and 2024, reflecting the contraction underway.137

NWT Budget 2026-27 totals $2.724 billion with no new taxes introduced.117 The Mining Incentive Program was updated with the $500,000 lifetime cap conditionally removed for corporate projects, while the $1.5 million annual budget was maintained.117 PM Carney announced a $35 billion+ Arctic defence and northern infrastructure plan including $32 billion at Forward Operating Locations in Yellowknife and Inuvik, plus the Mackenzie Highway extension.29

The Mackenzie Valley Highway â€” an 800+ km route from Wrigley to Norman Wells (Phase 1) and to Inuvik (Phase 2) â€” received construction approval with work starting summer 2026 and a revised cost estimate exceeding $2 billion.92 The Taltson Hydro Expansion ($2 billion proposed, 60 MW) would double the NWT's hydro capacity and deliver clean power to 11 communities serving approximately 70% of residents.122 The Pine Point zinc-lead mine ($653 million) is under review.49 The project database tracks 188 NWT projects and 52 energy-sector projects.3

provinces.name: Nunavut
provinces.analysis:
Nunavut's unemployment rate fell 3.0 percentage points to 10.8% in February 2026144, the largest single-month decline among all provinces and territories. The rate remains the highest in Canada, reflecting the structural employment constraints of a territory with 25 communities accessible only by air or seasonal sealift. The project database tracks 57 Nunavut projects, with 10 employment-sensitive projects.4

The federal government announced a $32 billion Northern Defence and Infrastructure investment covering Nunavut, including new Forward Operating Locations in Iqaluit and Northern Operation Support Nodes in Cambridge Bay and Rankin Inlet.30 Federal military hubs were also announced for Resolute.30 The federal Build Communities Strong Fund ($51 billion national) includes Nunavut allocations.123

Housing remains a central development constraint. The territory's target is 3,000 new units by 2030 with a $2.6 billion investment.121 The Nunavut 750 Homes Initiative â€” a tri-party agreement between the Government of Canada ($250 million), Government of Nunavut ($230 million), and Nunavut Tunngavik Incorporated â€” is under construction, with Baker Lake receiving the first 10 modular homes built by Ottawa manufacturer Caivan.56 Baffinland Iron Mines completed Inuit consultation for the Steensby Component of the Mary River project, clearing the final requirement to advance into construction at an estimated $3 billion.65 The Back River Gold Project ($610 million) is under construction in western Nunavut.49 Agnico Eagle operates as one of Nunavut's largest employers with over 2,000 positions, and gross mineral production exceeds $2.3 billion annually.121

Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector GDP stood at $47.2B in December 2025 and declined in January 2026, with decreases in both crop production and forestry.153 Crop production (except cannabis) fell 1.3% in November 2025, while forestry and logging declined 2.8% for the third consecutive month.153 Nutrien (NTR) closed at $104.62, up 50.6% year-over-year but down 1.0% week-over-week, reflecting sustained potash demand alongside near-term price softness.40 Canada exported 22.9 million tonnes of potash in 2024, accounting for over 39% of global exports.75

The project database tracks 17 agricultural projects ($5.47B), anchored by the BHP Jansen potash project in Saskatchewan ($10.6B total for Stage 1 and Stage 2), which is in full-scale construction with 5,500 construction-phase jobs and first production rescheduled to mid-CY2027.75 U.S.-Canada tariff disputes remain a factor for agricultural exports, with Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods continuing under the ongoing trade dispute.82 If trade disputes persist, agricultural export volumes face continued exposure to policy-driven disruption.

sections.industry_executive_summary:
Goods-producing industries recorded mixed results in January 2026. Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction expanded 1.2% month-over-month, while manufacturing contracted 1.4%.153 Construction and utilities both contributed to goods-sector gains. Agriculture declined, with crop production falling 1.3% and forestry and logging down 2.8% for a third consecutive month.153 The Strait of Hormuz closure drove WTI crude to US$102.88/bbl, the highest settlement since July 2022, directly affecting the 418 mining and energy projects tracked in the database.104

Services-producing industries were essentially unchanged in January 2026. Retail trade rose 0.8%, while wholesale trade declined 1.2%.153 Finance and insurance expanded, whereas real estate and professional services contracted. Transportation and warehousing declined, with extreme weather cited as a contributing factor.153 The February Labour Force Survey reported services-producing industries lost 56,000 positions, with wholesale and retail trade recording the largest subsector decline at 18,000 jobs.144 The project database tracks 7,372 projects across all sectors, with 1,034 under construction and 2,528 proposed.

financialMarkets.summary:
The Bank of Canada's Governing Council held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18, maintaining its stance following seven consecutive cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.67 The Governing Council stated it would "proceed carefully" given heightened uncertainty from US tariffs. Bond markets priced approximately 86% probability of no change at the April 15 meeting, with 14% probability of a 25-basis-point increase.68 The Government of Canada 2-year yield stood at 2.95% and the 10-year at 3.58%, producing a 2-10 year spread of 0.63 percentage points. Year-over-year, the yield curve shifted upward across all terms: the 2-year rose from 2.62% and the 10-year from 3.22%.

WTI crude surged to US$102.88/bbl, up more than 50% in March â€” the first settlement above $100 since July 2022 â€” driven by the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupting approximately 20 million barrels per day of seaborne oil flows.104 Brent crude settled at US$112.78/bbl, recording the largest monthly gain for the contract since inception in 1988.104 Natural gas (Henry Hub) traded at approximately US$3.05/MMBtu in late March; the EIA projects an average of $3.80 for 2026.11250 Gold declined approximately 14% in March to ~US$4,578/oz, the steepest monthly drop since October 2008, as margin liquidation and USD strength drove sellers.44 Copper traded in a range of US$5.25-$6.01/lb during March.60

The Canadian dollar weakened 1.85% month-over-month to 0.7198 CAD/USD (1.3893 USD/CAD), reflecting the 125-150 basis point spread between the Federal Reserve's 3.50-3.75% target and the BoC's 2.25%.58 The euro traded at 1.1460 EUR/USD, strengthening amid geopolitical uncertainty.114 The S&P/TSX Composite closed at 32,427 on March 31, up 1.54% on the day but down approximately 6% for March, while recording a 28.2% year-over-year gain.59 The S&P 500 closed at approximately 6,496, rallying 2.40% on March 31 â€” reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks contributed to the late-session advance â€” though the index remained approximately 9.4% below its January 2026 peak.61103

The Conference Board of Canada's consumer confidence index declined to 47.50 in February from 49.30 in January.57 The Bloomberg/Nanos Canadian Confidence Index recorded a three-week slide into late March, with the index moving toward the neutral threshold.48 The proportion of Canadians expecting the economy to strengthen in six months rose from 17% to 26% over the four-week period, according to Nanos Research.48 Rising energy costs â€” with WTI above $100/bbl for the first time since 2022 â€” and US trade friction were the most frequently cited sources of consumer anxiety in sentiment tracking.

Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, according to Statistics Canada.146 Motor vehicle and parts dealers led the increase at +2.0%, while general merchandise retailers posted a fourth consecutive monthly gain at +3.0%.14676 Core retail sales (excluding gasoline stations and motor vehicle dealers) increased 0.9%. E-commerce sales rose 1.5% to $4.4 billion, representing 6.2% of total retail trade.146 Alberta recorded the largest provincial retail increase at +3.5%, led by motor vehicle sales.76 The advance estimate for February retail sales is +0.9%.146 Statistics Canada's CPI report showed food inflation decelerating to 5.3% from 7.3% in January, while headline inflation fell to 1.8% year-over-year â€” the lowest since early 2021.14590

Canadian and global equity benchmarks advanced in the week ending April 9 — the S&P/TSX Composite closed at 33,478 (+1.12% W/W, +41.10% Y/Y)185, while the S&P 500 added +3.68% to 6,825186 and the Nikkei 225 gained +4.78% to 56,308202. The Canadian dollar firmed +0.70% to 0.7235 CAD/USD187, and the Bank of Canada held its policy rate at 2.25% for a seventh meeting73. The database tracks 5,644 active and proposed projects valued at $864.6 billion203.

Commodity moves split the pipeline along energy and metals lines — Brent crude fell -11.47% on the week to US$96.52/bbl, still +47.40% Y/Y184, against 28 oil and gas projects ($50.6B) and 207 power and energy projects ($328.1B)203. Gold settled at US$4,783/oz (+2.82%)189, copper at US$5.75/lb (+3.32%)190, and the Sprott uranium proxy at US$50.93 (+4.15%)191, referenced by 265 mining projects totalling $117.8B203. The 2s10s Government of Canada spread held at +63 bp with the 10-year at 3.58%177, against 657 rate-sensitive residential, commercial, and infrastructure projects ($76.4B)203.
yieldCurveCommentary: The Government of Canada yield curve held its normal upward-sloping shape on April 9, 2026, with the 2-year to 10-year spread at 63 basis points — the spread sits 3 basis points wider than the 60 basis point gap recorded one year ago177. The curve developed as the Bank of Canada overnight rate held at 2.25% for a seventh consecutive meeting, while long-end demand reflected the rotation into duration following the softer US labour data from the February 2026 release177197. The 2-year yield closed at 2.95%, up 33 basis points from 2.62% one year ago, while the 10-year yield closed at 3.58%, up 36 basis points from 3.22% one year ago177. The 30-year yield closed at 3.94%, up 41 basis points from 3.53% one year ago — the steepest year-over-year move across the six tenors carried in the Bank of Canada Valet feed since April 2025177. The 5-year to 10-year spread sits at 40 basis points177. If the 10-year yield holds near 3.58% amid the seventh consecutive Bank of Canada hold, The Signal Dispatch cross-reference engine links the 802 utilities projects tracked at C$507.7 billion and the 1,687 infrastructure projects tracked at C$179.0 billion to financing costs at the long end of the curve, while the 211 residential projects tracked at C$44.4 billion would retain exposure to the 2.95% 2-year benchmark204.
commodityCommentary: The week's commodity tape split between gains in precious metals and base metals on one side and weakness across energy on the other — gold added 2.82% to US$4,782.60/oz and copper rose 3.32% to US$5.75/lb, while Brent crude dropped 11.47% to US$96.52/bbl, the largest weekly Brent decline since the spring of 2025184189190. Henry Hub natural gas closed at US$2.67/MMBtu, the lowest weekly print since November 2024, driven by mild shoulder-season demand and elevated US storage carry188. Silver advanced 3.74% to US$75.46/oz, uranium proxy Sprott Physical Uranium Trust rose 4.15% to $50.93/share, and Nutrien (the potash proxy) declined 3.56% to $72.78/share, reflecting the rotation between hard commodities and fertilizer-linked names18919114. WTI is carried as N/A this week following a Phase 1A flag of a corrupt scrape; lumber, wheat, canola, and nickel are similarly carried as N/A on stale or corrupt feeds.
